II. ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}+{x}_{4}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\mathbf{0}$ has only zero solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0$

II and III only
I only
II only

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, solving equation ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}=3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-2{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+5{\mathbf{v}}_{3}$ for ${\mathbf{v}}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}.
$$

This means that ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$, ${\mathbf{v}}_{3},$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}.$

- Statement II is false. Since ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}=3{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-2{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+5{\mathbf{v}}_{3},$ we have that

$$
3\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{1}-2\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{2}+5\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{3}+(-1)\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

As a result, ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}+{x}_{4}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\mathbf{0}$ has a non-zero solution.

- Statement III is false. Since ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}+{x}_{4}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\mathbf{0}$ has a non-zero solution, the set $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}\}$ is a linearly dependent set by definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){\mathbf{v}}_{2}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}){\mathbf{v}}_{3} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}\}$ is a linearly independent set, the final equation can be true only if

$$
\begin{cases}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0.\end{cases}
$$

The unique solution of the system is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ which means that 

$$
\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}\}

 is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, notice that

$$
1\cdot \mathbf{0}+0\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{1}+0\cdot (2{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{0}.

As a result, ${x}_{1}\mathbf{0}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{3}(2{\mathbf{v}}_{2})=\mathbf{0}$ has a non-zero solution. This means that $\{\mathbf{0},{\mathbf{v}}_{1},2{\mathbf{v}}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent. In general, any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}$ must have only the zero solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$  If this equation has a non-zero solution, $a\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{1}+b\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0},$ then we obtain

I. $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}\}$ is linearly independent

II. $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}-{\mathbf{v}}_{1}\}$ is linearly independent

III. $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent

choices.html: III only
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II, and III

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is true. Suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2})+{x}_{2}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{3})+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which, in turn, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){\mathbf{v}}_{1}+({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}){\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{3} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}\}$ is a linearly independent set, the final equation can be true only if

$$
\begin{cases}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0.\end{cases}
$$

The unique solution of the system is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ which means that 

$$
\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}\}
$$

 is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, notice that

$$
1\cdot ({\mathbf{v}}_{1}-{\mathbf{v}}_{2})+1\cdot ({\mathbf{v}}_{2}-{\mathbf{v}}_{1})=\mathbf{0}.
$$

As a result, ${x}_{1}({\mathbf{v}}_{1}-{\mathbf{v}}_{2})+{x}_{2}({\mathbf{v}}_{2}-{\mathbf{v}}_{1})=\mathbf{0}$ has a non-zero solution. This means that $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1}-{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}-{\mathbf{v}}_{1}\}$ is linearly dependent.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}$ must have only the zero solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$  If this equation has a non-zero solution, $a\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{1}+b\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0},$ then we obtain

$$
a\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{1}+b\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{2}+0\cdot {\mathbf{v}}_{3}=\mathbf{0},
$$

which would mean that $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

I. ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ is a linear combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$, ${\mathbf{v}}_{3}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}$

II. ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{3}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}$

III. ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{\mathbf{v}}_{3}$ is a linear combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}\}$ is a linearly dependent set, we obtain that

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}+{x}_{4}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has a non-zero solution. Moreover, ${x}_{1}$ can't be zero because then

$$
{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}+{x}_{4}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\mathbf{0}
$$

will have a non-zero solution and that's a contradiction as $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}\}$ is linearly independent.
Therefore, from ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}+{x}_{4}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\mathbf{0},$ we get

$$
{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=-\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}-\frac{{x}_{3}}{{x}_{1}}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}-\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{1}}{\mathbf{v}}_{4}.
$$

This means that ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ is a linear combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$, ${\mathbf{v}}_{3},$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}.$

- Statement II is false. Since $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}\}$ is a linearly independent set, ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ can not be a linear combination of other vectors.

- Statement III is false. Since $\{{\mathbf{v}}_{2},{\mathbf{v}}_{3},{\mathbf{v}}_{4}\}$ is a linearly independent set, ${\mathbf{v}}_{3}$ can not be a linear combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}.$ As a result ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{\mathbf{v}}_{3}$ can't be written as combination of ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{4}$ too.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \in V.$ Given that $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is linearly independent, which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{ 4\mathbf{v}_1, 5\mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is linearly independent

II. $\{ \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{v}_1, 2\mathbf{v}_2 \}$ is linearly independent

III. $\{ \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \}$ is linearly independent
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is true. Suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(4{\mathbf{v}}_{1})+{x}_{2}(5{\mathbf{v}}_{2})+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3} & =\mathbf{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which, in turn, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(4{x}_{1}){\mathbf{v}}_{1}+(5{x}_{2}){\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is a linearly independent set, the final equation can be true only if

$$
\begin{cases}4{x}_{1}=0 \\ 5{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{cases}
$$

The unique solution of the system is $x_1=x_2=x_3=0,$ which means that 

$$
\{ 4\mathbf{v}_1, 5\mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}
$$

 is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, notice that

$$
1 \cdot \mathbf{0} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 + 0 \cdot (2\mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

As a result, $x_1\mathbf{0}+x_2\mathbf{v}_1+x_3(2\mathbf{v}_2)=\mathbf{0}$ has a non-zero solution. This means that $\{ \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{v}_1, 2\mathbf{v}_2 \}$ is linearly dependent. In general, any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, $x_1\mathbf{v}_2+x_2\mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{0}$ must have only the zero solution $x_1=x_2=0.$  If this equation has a non-zero solution, $a \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 + b \cdot \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{0},$ then we obtain

$$
0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 + a \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 + b \cdot \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0},
$$

which would mean that $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is linearly dependent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

solution_sources.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ not both zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B=O.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A$ and $B$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ -1 & 10\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 2 & -12\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 5{x}_{1} \\ -{x}_{1} & 10{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{2} & 6{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} & -12{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} & 5{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & 10{x}_{1}-12{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{cases}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}-12{x}_{2}=0\end{cases}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ not all zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{1} \\ 0 & -2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} & -{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} & 4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} & -4{x}_{3} \\ -8{x}_{3} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3} & -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{cases}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0.\end{cases}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 & 0\end{array}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 & 0\end{array}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd.
Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

The system is now

$$
\begin{cases}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0.\end{cases}
$$

From the $2$nd equation, we get ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substitute it into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-3(4{x}_{3})+4{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=8{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Finally, for any ${x}_{3}\ne 0,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=\frac{8{x}_{3}}{4{x}_{3}}=2.
$$

$$

$$

Consequently, $\{A,B\}$ is linearly independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2t-4{t}^{2})+{x}_{2}(3t-6{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ (2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})t+(-4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in \mathbb{R}.

Finally, for any ${x}_{2}\ne 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{(-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2})}=-\frac{2}{3}.

$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ not both zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2{t}^{2}+t+4)+{x}_{2}(4t-1) & =0 \\ 2{t}^{2}{x}_{1}+({x}_{1}+4{x}_{2})t+(4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\begin{cases}2{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0.\end{cases}
$$

From the first equation we obtain ${x}_{1}=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ 

Therefore, $\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is linearly independent.
